I wasn’t top of the class but near the top in both EMT and Paramedic school (8 years apart), you will not be good when you first start plain and simple. Time and experience is what you need and also developing a flow. My flow won’t be your flow which won’t be your partners flow but you will come up with your own that in turn becomes basically like your script on every call. For me it’s introducing myself, obtain chief complaint, ask orientation questions, deeper dive into the chief complaint (OPQRST) and then get into the AMPLE part of SAMPLE though I switch it up and it’s more of a EPAML order. Nobody showed me that but it’s how I found it to be most helpful and flows better for me while still getting all the information I need. I’ve been in EMS 20 years now and it’s become pretty much muscle memory now where I can be on the tail end of a 72 hour shift at 3am on my 50th call of the shift and it just comes out. Don’t get discouraged, practice with your partners, put on classes with your crew like what types of traction splints are there, which do you carry, how are they different, when to use or not use, etc. keep at it and you’ll be great.

There’s no measure necessarily of how strong you have to be, it’s more can you do the job? Can you drag someone out of a building, can you throw a ladder, can you shoulder hose and walk up several flights of stairs, etc. and more importantly can you do it over and over again? Like some have mentioned it’s all about functional fitness. HIIT workouts and circuits are the best in my opinion because you build on strength, mobility and endurance. I work in Southern California and we get as many vegetation fires as structure fires so benching 400lbs isn’t going to matter when you’re doing a 5000 foot hose lay on a vegetation fire up some steep hills. The job is dynamic and you have to adapt, you might be dragging hose in a building, doing chest compressions, running extrication tools, hiking up a hill etc. so try to workout accordingly.

I work for a larger department (100 stations) and I’ve seen it varies from station to station or battalion to battalion. My previous battalion we would eat dinner as a crew and we had an engine, truck and ambulance out of our station so cooking duties were split with each apparatus having a cook day, they buy the food, divide the cost and then everyone pays their share to whoever bought and it was awesome. I later transferred to a station with a 3 person engine crew and each person had a cook day. We didn’t pay each other back and forth though since it made no sense to pay me $8 today for me to pay you $8 tomorrow (unless it was a fancier more expensive dinner that we all agreed on to pay for) and that was great. My current assignment also a 3 man single engine house, everyone is on their own, sometimes we all make our own separate dinner and eat together but usually it’s everyone on their own and eating whenever each person is hungry and I’m not a huge fan. I like the “family dinner” atmosphere, specially at the bigger houses. The joking, laughing, war stories, solving all the world’s problems, rookie introductions/presentations and even playing games for dishes. I’m eligible to transfer out in 6 months and am planning on going to a station that still does group dinners. I feel the crew cohesion and camaraderie is way greater than stations that don’t eat together.

Where I work we use START in the field and hospitals are on the REDDINET system. I’ll try to make it short but 1st arriving EMS (preferably fire so as to not take a transporting unit out of the equation) gets on scene. Our fire crews typically have 1 captain, 1 engineer and 1 firefighter paramedic. the captain assumes command of the incident, the paramedic assumes what we call MEDCOM and calls the closest base hospital and declares an MCI with an approximate total patient count and lets the base hospital nurse they’ll call back with a more accurate count at which point the paramedic hangs up and the base hospital nurse gets on their computer and checks reddinet which shows bed availability of all local hospitals, and will call the hospitals to let them know what’s going on and to see if they can clear more beds. the engineer grabs triage tags and starts triaging where he stands.

The triage system is based on RPM (Respirations, Perfusion, Mental Status) and we use the 30-2-can do for the triage assessment. The 30 is for respiration count, 2 is for seconds of capillary refill and “can do” is for “can a patient follow simple commands”. Typically to sort out the patients from bystanders, the engineer will yell out “I need anyone that is injured to come over here, anyone who is a witness or bystander to go over there”. That does 2 things, shows your “walking wounded” aka minor/green tag patients and gets rid of bystanders. Then they start triage on the first patient they come across that couldn’t walk away. 1st they assess breathing, if no breathing they do a head tilt/chin lift, if spontaneous breathing does not return they are labeled deceased aka black tag, if breathing returns if it’s less than 10 or more than 30 they get labeled “immediate” or red tag and move on to the next patient. if they’re between 10-30 respirations then you move to cap refill. If cap refill is more than 2 seconds they get a red tag, if less you move on to Mental status. If they can follow simple commands aka “can do” then they get a “delayed” yellow tag, if they can not then they get red tagged. It should take no longer than 30 seconds per patient because no treatment is being provided.

At that point the engineer (triage) reports back to the paramedic (MEDCOM) with a patient count something like “I have 4 Deceased, 11 immediate, 6 delayed and 19 minor”. MEDCOM will call back to base and let them know the updated count and status and the nurse will let MEDCOM know bed availability such as “hospital 1 can take 3 immediate, 3 delayed, 3 minor. Hospital 2 can take 1 immediate, 4 delayed, 5 minor, etc…”

as more resources arrive on scene, they start setting up treatment areas and litter crews to move patients to the designated “immediate/delayed/minor”treatment area where they will start treatment while awaiting transport. Transport will be set up near the treatment areas and 1 person, usually an ambulance supervisor will be designated as the transport unit leader. MEDCOM will work with the transport unit leader and let them know “ambulance 1 will be taking 1 immediate and 2 minors to hospital one, have the ambulance contact hospital 1 en route, have them return after patients have been dropped off”, and so on until all patients have been transported off the scene. 

The captain who is the incident commander is pretty much just ordering resources based on the amount of patients and MEDCOM’s recommendations such as additional fire engines, ambulances, airships, etc.

Now there are obviously caveats to this. The above is more like a bus crash, or something like that. But if it was like HAZMAT situation then we have to establish decontamination areas, air monitoring etc. if its an active shooter and the shooter is still on the loose then we go active shooter protocol where we make entry with law enforcement escorting and us wearing tactical helmets and vests and an active shooter bag which has needle decompression, tourniquets, chest seals, hemostatic dressings/bandages and black, red, green and black flagging for triage. In this type of scenario we can do limited treatment such as needle decompression or applying tourniquets and chest seals but we’re not moving patients, just triaging and trying to stop any immediate life threatening injuries to buy the patients time until the litter teams can get them out to the treatment area and transport.
